transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well, my regular doctor told me I needed to come here. He says I've gotten too thin. I mean, I guess I can see my work pants hanging loose on me lately. They're these stiff navy trousers they make the cleaning staff wear at the municipal building. Honestly, the fabric is so scratchy, and the heating in that building is completely broken half the time. Last week I was shivering my whole shift, and I keep telling the supervisor they need to fix the radiators in the east wing, but they never listen to the night crew. It’s always been like that with city buildings, even when I was taking night classes at the community college years ago, the heating in those classrooms was just awful. You'd sit there in your coat trying to take notes. 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the doctor. Yeah, he's worried because the pants are bagging off me. But to be perfectly honest with you... even though they're loose, part of me still feels relieved when the number on the scale is lower.
Have you been intentionally trying to lose weight or change your body shape, or do you find yourself preoccupied with your weight or appearance?

Well, I don't know about "preoccupied," but I do like to keep things... tidy. You know? When I stay small and neat, I just feel like I'm handling everything right. It's like my work, I take a lot of pride in keeping things neat. Like the big glass doors and mirrors in the main lobby at the municipal building. I spend half my shift just getting the streaks out of those things because people can't seem to keep their hands off the glass. 

Especially the kids. They put a daycare on the first floor a few years back, which makes absolutely no sense for a government building. The zoning board must have lost their minds approving that. Sticky little fingerprints everywhere, all over the lower half of the glass, every single day. I actually use this special ammonia mix my grandmother taught me about, it cuts right through the grease so much better than that cheap blue stuff the city buys in bulk... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, my appearance. Yeah, well... like I said, I just like being small and neat. If I catch a glimpse of myself in one of those lobby mirrors and my stomach looks the least bit full, I just feel like I've completely let myself go. It just feels wrong, like I'm not doing my job right, you know?
Do you have a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though others might see you as underweight?

Well, I wouldn't call it a fear, exactly. It's more just... a panic. Like, if I eat something heavier, you know? Like biscuits or pasta. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she's always trying to bring over these heavy baked ziti dishes. She's a sweet lady, but she uses entirely too much cheese. I keep telling her, "Mildred, you're going to give yourself a heart attack with all that ricotta," but she just waves me off. She says her husband loved it, God rest his soul. He passed away about five years ago, bless him. He was a nice man, used to help me shovel my driveway in the winter when my snowblower would act up. I really need to get that snowblower serviced before December, the spark plug is completely shot and the guy at the hardware store said they don't make that exact part anymore, so I have to order it special online...

I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the weight. Yes. If I eat something like that pasta, I spend the rest of the day just... scared that it's going to show on me immediately. I keep checking myself in the mirror, pulling at my clothes, thinking I need to make up for it somehow. I just can't stand the thought of getting bigger.
After eating, do you ever make yourself exercise, restrict food, or do anything else to prevent weight gain?

Well, I wouldn't say I make myself do anything, really. I just... I like to stay active. It's good for you, right? At my age, you have to keep moving or your joints just freeze up on you. My sister Margaret, she's two years older than me, and she can barely get up the stairs in her house anymore because of her knees. She had that replacement surgery last fall, but the physical therapist said she didn't do her exercises right, so now she's worse off than before. I keep telling her she needs to walk, just around the block, but she says her neighborhood isn't safe for walking anymore. They put in a new traffic light at the corner of Elm and Main, and people just fly through it on the yellow. It's terrible. I almost got clipped there myself last week when I was walking to the grocery store. I always walk to the store, it's only a mile, and... 

Oh, right, after eating. No, I don't really do anything special like that. I just go about my day, you know? Keep moving. Keep busy. I don't really restrict anything or... do anything else. Just stay busy.
Have you ever made yourself vomit or used laxatives, diet pills, or diuretics to control your weight or shape after eating?

No, no, I've never done anything like that. Vomiting is just awful, isn't it? It ruins your teeth, for one thing. My dentist, Dr. Aris, he's always talking about enamel. He's this young guy, just took over the practice from Dr. Miller who retired down to Florida. Naples, I think. Or maybe Sarasota. Somewhere on the Gulf Coast. Anyway, Dr. Aris has this huge saltwater fish tank in his waiting room, and I swear those fish look stressed. You can tell when a fish is stressed, their colors get all dull. I had a goldfish when I was a little girl, won him at the county fair by tossing a ping pong ball into a fishbowl. My mother was furious because she had to go buy a proper tank and a filter and all that. We named him Barnaby, and he lived for five years, which is practically a century for a fair goldfish...

What did you ask me? Laxatives and things? No, no. I don't take any of those pills or anything. I just keep things tidy. Just keep moving, like I said.
Do you judge yourself mainly based on your body weight or shape?

Well, I suppose I do, yes. It's just about being tidy, really. When I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right, you know? Like I'm keeping everything in order. It's like when I clean the floors at the middle school where I work. I've been there for fifteen years now. The kids are messy, of course, especially in the cafeteria. They drop those little milk cartons and they explode everywhere. And the smell of sour milk, oh, it's just impossible to get out of the linoleum if you don't mop it up right away. The principal, Mr. Henderson, he's a stickler for the floors. He always says, "A clean floor is a happy school," which is a bit silly if you ask me, but he means well. He's retiring next year, actually. Going to spend more time with his grandkids in Ohio. I've never been to Ohio. I hear it's very flat... 

Oh, right, judging myself. Yes, well, if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror, I just feel like I've let myself go. Like I'm not doing my job right, keeping myself neat. It just feels wrong.
Do your thoughts about your weight or shape interfere with your daily life, such as affecting your work, relationships, or other important activities?

Well, I still get my cleaning shifts done at the school, of course. I'd never let my work slip. The buffing machine we use, it's this old industrial thing, heavy as a tractor. You really have to lean into it to keep it steady, otherwise it pulls you right across the hallway. The new guy, Tommy, he started last month and he nearly took out a row of lockers his first time using it. I told him, you have to guide it from your hips, not your shoulders. He's a nice kid, though. Reminds me of my nephew David. David's over in Seattle now, working for one of those computer companies. He sends us coffee beans sometimes, these fancy roasts that smell like blueberries. My husband, Arthur, he can't stand them. He just wants his Folgers from a can, like he's had for forty years...

Oh, you were asking about my daily life and things. Well, I do avoid family dinners now, and the potlucks at church. I just can't sit there with all those casseroles and heavy dishes. Arthur says I'm around everyone without really joining in anymore. But I just prefer to keep things tidy, you know? It's easier if I just stay out of the kitchen when everyone's eating.
When you look at yourself in the mirror, do you feel like you appear overweight or larger than you actually are?

Well, no, not really. I don't think I look larger than I am. I just see what's there, you know? I just see where things aren't quite as tidy as they should be. It's like when you're looking at a window that hasn't been washed properly. You can see the streaks right away if the light hits it just right. We have these huge windows in the school library, facing east, so the morning sun just blasts right through them. If I don't use the squeegee exactly right, Mrs. Gable—she's the librarian—she'll point out every single smudge. She's got these thick glasses on a chain around her neck, and she'll peer over them at the glass. She's been reading this new mystery series, something about a baker who solves murders in a small town in Vermont. I tried reading one once, but I just couldn't get into it. I prefer biographies, real people, you know? I read a fascinating one about Eleanor Roosevelt last winter when we had that big snowstorm and the power was out for two days. Arthur had to get the generator running just so we wouldn't freeze... 

What was I saying about the mirror? Oh. No, I don't think I look overweight. I just see the parts that need work. The parts that aren't neat yet.
When you look at yourself in the mirror, do you feel like you appear overweight or larger than you actually are?

I think we just... didn't I just say? Well, like I mentioned, no, I don't think I look bigger than I really am. I just see the parts that aren't quite right yet. 

Speaking of mirrors, though, Arthur has this terrible magnifying mirror in our bathroom for his shaving. It has this little fluorescent ring light around the edge that constantly flickers because the bulb is going bad. It gives me an absolute headache. I told him to go down to the hardware store—Miller's Hardware, over on 4th street—to get a replacement, but he insists they don't make that specific size anymore. Mr. Miller is such a nice man, though. He helped me find the exact right grit of sandpaper when I was refinishing that old rocking chair we found at the estate sale last spring. The one with the spindle back? It took me three entire weekends to get through all the old varnish. The dust gets absolutely everywhere, right up into your nose, even if you wear one of those paper masks. I had to sweep the garage floor twice a day just to keep it from tracking into the house... 

But yes, to answer your question again, no. I don't see myself as overweight. I just see what needs to be tidied up.
When you look at yourself in the mirror, do you ever feel like you look bigger or more overweight than you actually are?

Are you... are you asking me the same thing again? I feel like we're going in circles here, doctor. I really don't think I look bigger. I just see the parts that need to be fixed, like I said. 

It's funny how things go in circles, though. The buffing machine at work, it goes in circles, and if you don't hold it just right, it leaves these terrible swirl marks on the linoleum. We use this special wax, comes in a big five-gallon bucket. Smells like lemons and chemicals. Reminds me of the lemonade stand my granddaughter, Lily, set up last summer. She made $14 and spent it all on those little plastic horses you get at the toy store. She has a whole collection of them now, lines them up on her windowsill. The windowsill that Arthur still hasn't fixed the draft on, mind you. Winter is coming and I just know we're going to have a terrible time keeping the heating bill down... 

But yes, doctor. For the third time, no. I don't feel like I look overweight.
Would you say that your overall sense of how well you're doing in life is strongly connected to how you feel about your body shape or weight?

Well, yes, I suppose it is. When I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right, you know? Like things are under control. But if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror, I feel like I've just let myself go completely. It's a terrible feeling. Like dropping a whole tray of glasses. 

Which actually happened to me once, back when I was taking classes at the community college. I was waitressing at this little diner on Route 9 to pay for my textbooks. The textbooks were so expensive, even back then. I remember my biology book alone was almost fifty dollars. It had this glossy cover with a picture of a cell dividing. Mitosis, I think it's called? Anyway, I was carrying this huge tray of water glasses to a big table of truckers, and my foot caught the edge of a floor mat that hadn't been taped down right. The whole thing went crashing. Glass everywhere, water all over the linoleum. The manager, Mr. Henderson, he was furious. He had this little mustache that would twitch when he got mad. He made me sweep it all up, and then mop the whole dining room before I could go home. I didn't get out of there until almost two in the morning. And Arthur was waiting up for me, worried sick because this was before cell phones, of course. He had made a pot of coffee that was practically sludge by the time I got back...

But yes, if I don't look neat and small, I feel like everything is just a mess. Like I'm failing at it all.
Would you say that your overall sense of self-worth is strongly connected to how you feel about your body shape or weight?

I feel like... didn't you just ask me that? Or something exactly like it? We were just talking about this, doctor. Yes, my body shape matters a lot to how I feel about myself. If I'm not keeping myself small, I just feel awful, like I'm not doing a good job at anything. 

It's sort of like when I'm doing the floors at the office building. If I miss a spot, the whole hallway looks wrong to me. Even if nobody else notices, I know it's there. Just like that stain on the carpet in the lobby of the third floor. I've tried everything on it. Club soda, vinegar, that expensive foaming spray they buy us from the supply catalog. Nothing gets it out completely. It's from when someone dropped a cup of blackberry tea, I think. Blackberries are terrible for staining. My grandmother used to make blackberry preserves every August, and our fingers would be purple for a week. She had this huge copper kettle she'd boil them in on the stove. The kitchen would get so hot, just stifling, because she wouldn't open the windows. She said the draft would ruin the set of the jam. I still have some of her old mason jars down in the basement, the ones with the glass lids and the wire clamps... 

But yes, to answer your question again, how I feel about my weight is basically how I feel about myself. If I'm not small, I'm just not doing well.
When you look at yourself, do you ever feel like your body or certain parts of it appear larger than they actually are?

Doctor, I really... I feel like you're not listening to me. You asked me this exact same thing about the mirror and looking bigger just a few minutes ago. I don't see things larger than they are, I just see what needs to be fixed. I don't know how many different ways I can say it. 

It's like trying to explain to the new girl at work, Sarah, about the buffing pads. She keeps using the red ones on the tile when she should be using the white ones. The red ones are too abrasive, they strip the finish right off. I told her three times last week, but she's always got those little white earbuds in, listening to podcasts or whatever it is young people listen to. My granddaughter Lily wants a pair of those for Christmas, but Arthur says they're too expensive for a ten-year-old. He's probably right. He usually is about money. He's been keeping our ledger in the same green notebook since 1985. Every penny accounted for. I remember when we bought our first car, a used Ford Fairmont, it was a terrible mustard yellow color, but it ran like a top... 

Anyway, no. I don't see my body as larger than it is. Just like I said before.
Do you feel like certain foods cause you to gain weight immediately, even if you've only eaten a small amount?

Oh, absolutely. If I eat something heavier, like, say, a biscuit or some pasta, I just... I spend the rest of the day terrified it's going to show right on me. Even just a little bite. Arthur loves biscuits, actually. He buys those ones in the cardboard tube from the supermarket, the ones that pop really loud when you peel the paper back. I hate opening them, it always startles me so badly. It sounds exactly like a firecracker. 

My older brother, Thomas, he used to set off firecrackers in empty Folgers coffee cans on the Fourth of July when we were kids. He actually blew the metal mailbox right off the wooden post one year. My dad was just beside himself. He chased Thomas all the way down the driveway with a rolled-up newspaper. Dad was always reading the paper, the Sunday edition especially, looking for the hardware store circulars. He'd sit in this awful plaid recliner, green and brown, and smoke his pipe. It smelled like cherry vanilla, which was nice, but the smoke absolutely ruined the living room curtains. My mother was always having to wash those curtains. She had an old wringer washer down in the cellar, and you had to be so careful not to get your fingers caught in the rollers. She did once, and her nail turned completely black...

But, well, what I mean is, if I eat a biscuit or something heavy like that, I just feel so scared. I keep checking myself in the mirror, over and over, just looking to see if the weight is already there. And I just keep thinking about how I need to make up for it, you know? Like I have to fix it right away or I'll just keep expanding.
Do you ever engage in any specific behaviors—like fasting, following strict diets, or doing extra exercise—to make up for eating something you consider heavy or fattening?

No, I don't really do any extra exercise or fasting or anything like that. I just try not to eat those heavy things to begin with. Besides, I'm on my feet all night at the building anyway. Pushing that heavy cleaning cart around is enough of a workout for anybody. 

Though I will say, the cart they gave me for the second floor has this awful squeaky front wheel. It squeaks every single time I turn a corner, and it drives me absolutely up the wall. I asked Gary, the maintenance supervisor, to put some WD-40 on it three weeks ago. Gary is a nice enough guy, but he's so forgetful these days. He just got this new golden retriever puppy, and that's all he talks about now. He just stands in the hallway showing everyone pictures of it chewing on his slippers on his phone. 

My husband Arthur and I had a dog when we were first married, a little beagle named Buster. He was an absolute terror, honestly. He dug up all of my petunias in the front yard the very first spring we had him. I had worked so hard on that flower bed, hauling heavy bags of mulch in the trunk of that old yellow Fairmont I told you about... the trunk latch was sticky on that car, so you had to bang on it with the side of your fist just to get it open. Arthur finally fixed it with a piece of wire he found in the garage, but it always looked a little funny after that. 

But no, what was it you asked? Making up for eating? No, I don't do anything extra like that. I'm not sure what you mean, really. I just do my normal routine.
Do you ever skip meals, fast, or follow an extremely strict diet to control your weight or shape?

Well, I don't really think of it as a strict diet or fasting. I do cook, you know. I make nice, full plates for my husband and my mother-in-law every evening. But by the time I actually sit down at the table with them, I usually just tell myself that some coffee, or maybe a few vegetables or half a piece of toast is enough for me. 

Speaking of toast, Arthur's mother—she lives with us now—she insists on having her toast practically burnt to a crisp. I mean, absolutely blackened. It sets off the smoke detector in the hallway at least twice a week. That alarm has this awful, piercing shriek... and it's one of those hardwired ones, so you can't just pull the nine-volt battery out to make it stop. Arthur was trying to fan the smoke away with a heavy dish towel last Tuesday and he ended up knocking my ceramic rooster right off the top of the refrigerator. It shattered into a million pieces. 

I was so upset about that. I bought that rooster at the Canton flea market back in... oh, it must have been 1998. We took a weekend trip up there because the leaves were just starting to turn those beautiful reds and oranges. We stopped at this little roadside diner on the way home, and they had this old jukebox in the corner that still played 45s. Arthur played a Patsy Cline song for me. He used to be so romantic like that before his knees started giving him trouble...
Do your concerns about staying small and neat ever cause you to avoid social situations or feel anxious around other people?

Well, I... I suppose it does, yes. I still get all my cleaning shifts done at the building, of course. I'm very reliable that way. But when it comes to being around people... I avoid family dinners now. And the potlucks after church, I just can't do those anymore. My husband, Arthur, he says I'm physically around everyone but I'm not really joining in. 

It's just so hard with the church potlucks, you know? Everyone brings these huge casserole dishes. Mrs. Higgins always brings her green bean casserole with those crispy fried onions on top. She uses the French's brand, the ones in the little plastic canister. I know because I saw her buying them at the Piggly Wiggly last Tuesday. I was in the checkout line behind her, and the cashier, a young girl with bright purple hair—can you imagine, purple hair?—she was having the hardest time getting the barcode scanner to work. It just kept beeping and beeping, this awful high-pitched noise. It reminded me of the time the backup alarm got stuck on the garbage truck outside our house. It went on for two hours before the sanitation workers finally figured out how to shut it off. 

That was the same day Arthur decided he was going to try and fix the leaky faucet in the downstairs bathroom by himself. He watched a video on the computer, but he ended up stripping the threading on the pipe, and water just went everywhere. It soaked right through the bathmat. It was one of those memory foam ones, light blue, and it took three days to dry out completely. We had to hang it over the railing on the back deck, and the neighbor's cat, a big orange tabby named Marmalade, kept trying to sleep on it... 

But, yes, what Arthur says is true. I'm there at the table, or at the church hall, but I'm not really... participating. It's just easier to stay away from the food, and I guess that means staying away from the socializing, too.
Would you say that being small and neat is not just a preference for you, but something you feel you *must* be in order to feel good about yourself or like you're doing life right?

Oh, absolutely. It's not just a preference. When I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right, you know? Like I'm keeping everything in order. But if I look in the mirror and my stomach looks the least bit full, I just feel like I've completely let myself go. 

Speaking of mirrors, the one we have in our hallway has this awful distortion right near the bottom. Arthur bought it at a garage sale over on Elm Street last summer. The man running the sale was selling all his ex-wife's things, which I thought was a bit spiteful, honestly. He had all these beautiful old glass lamps just sitting out on folding tables in the hot sun. Anyway, Arthur brought this heavy mirror home and tried to fix the chipped wooden frame with some mahogany wood stain he found in the basement. 

He ended up dripping it right onto our beige hallway carpet. It left this dark reddish-brown spot that looks exactly like a squashed cherry. I tried scrubbing it out with that foaming carpet cleaner—the one in the aerosol can with the little plastic brush attached to the lid? But the brush bristles were entirely too stiff and it just frayed the carpet fibers. Now we just keep a little potted fern over the spot so nobody sees it. The fern isn't doing too well, though. The leaves keep turning yellow on the edges. My mother-in-law keeps pouring her leftover tea into the pot, and I've told her a hundred times the tannins are too acidic for the soil, but she never listens to me... 

But yes, if I see any fullness at all when I'm getting dressed, I just feel like a failure. I have to keep it all neat.

But, yes, what Arthur says is true. I'm there at the table, or at the church hall, but I'm not really... participating. It's just easier to stay away from the food, and I guess that means staying away from the socializing, too.

doctor.question: Would you say that being small and neat is not just a preference for you, but something you feel you *must* be in order to feel good about yourself or like you're doing life right?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right, but if my stomach looks the least bit full in the mirror I feel like I've let myself go.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks if the patient's need to be "small and neat" is something she feels she *must* be to feel good about herself or like she's doing life right, which maps exactly to the Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. It's not just a preference. When I stay small and neat, I feel like I'm handling everything right, you know? Like I'm keeping everything in order. But if I look in the mirror and my stomach looks the least bit full, I just feel like I've completely let myself go. 

Speaking of mirrors, the one we have in our hallway has this awful distortion right near the bottom. Arthur bought it at a garage sale over on Elm Street last summer. The man running the sale was selling all his ex-wife's things, which I thought was a bit spiteful, honestly. He had all these beautiful old glass lamps just sitting out on folding tables in the hot sun. Anyway, Arthur brought this heavy mirror home and tried to fix the chipped wooden frame with some mahogany wood stain he found in the basement. 

He ended up dripping it right onto our beige hallway carpet. It left this dark reddish-brown spot that looks exactly like a squashed cherry. I tried scrubbing it out with that foaming carpet cleaner—the one in the aerosol can with the little plastic brush attached to the lid? But the brush bristles were entirely too stiff and it just frayed the carpet fibers. Now we just keep a little potted fern over the spot so nobody sees it. The fern isn't doing too well, though. The leaves keep turning yellow on the edges. My mother-in-law keeps pouring her leftover tea into the pot, and I've told her a hundred times the tannins are too acidic for the soil, but she never listens to me... 

But yes, if I see any fullness at all when I'm getting dressed, I just feel like a failure. I have to keep it all neat.
